Autodiff Future Work - Implementation Roadmap

Current Status (Completed ✅)

What's Working Now

  1. Fully generic workspace - Supports ForwardDiff.Dual numbers
  2. Workspace caching - Eliminates allocation overhead
  3. Automatic sparsity pattern - Fast detection from model structure
  4. Sparse colored Jacobian - Production-ready performance

Performance Benchmarks

IEEE 14-bus system (28 variables):

  • Jacobian: ~2ms (after warmup)
  • Sparsity: 98.4% efficient
  • 2.8x speedup from coloring

ACTIVSg 70k-bus system (135,800 variables):

  • Jacobian: ~140ms (after warmup)
  • Sparsity: 99.996% sparse
  • 1,717x speedup vs dense
  • 34 colors (from 135,800 columns)

Remaining Future Work

Priority 1: Production Integration (High Value, Medium Effort)

1.1 NonlinearSolve.jl Integration

Goal: High-level API for users who want automatic everything.

Implementation:

Create src/solvers/nonlinear_solve.jl:

using NonlinearSolve

"""
    solve_power_flow(sys::SystemModel;
                    method=NewtonRaphson(),
                    autodiff=AutoSparseForwardDiff(),
                    tol=1e-8,
                    maxiter=20)

Solve power flow using NonlinearSolve.jl with automatic differentiation.

# Example
\```julia
sys = SystemModel(am, models)
sol = solve_power_flow(sys)
\```
"""
function solve_power_flow(
    sys::SystemModel;
    method=NewtonRaphson(),
    autodiff=AutoSparseForwardDiff(),
    tol=1e-8,
    maxiter=20
)
    # Create cached workspace
    cache = CachedAutodiffWorkspace(sys)

    # Get sparsity pattern
    sparsity = jacobian_sparsity_pattern(sys)

    # Create NonlinearFunction with sparsity info
    nlfunc = NonlinearFunction(
        cache;
        jac_prototype = float.(sparsity)
    )

    # Create problem
    prob = NonlinearProblem(nlfunc, copy(cache.sys.dae.y))

    # Solve
    sol = solve(prob, method; autodiff=autodiff, abstol=tol, maxiters=maxiter)

    return sol
end

Files to modify:

  • Create src/solvers/nonlinear_solve.jl
  • Add to src/Powerful.jl: include("solvers/nonlinear_solve.jl")
  • Export solve_power_flow

Dependencies: Add to Project.toml:

NonlinearSolve = "8913a72c-1f9b-4ce2-8d82-65094dcecaec"

Testing:

# test/test_nonlinear_solve.jl
@testitem "NonlinearSolve.jl Integration" begin
    using Powerful, PowerFlowData

    case = PowerFlowData.parse_network(joinpath(pkgdir(Powerful), "cases", "ieee14.raw"))
    bus = parse_model(Bus, case)
    pq = parse_model(PQ, case)
    pv = parse_model(PV, case)
    branch = parse_model(Branch, case)

    sys = SystemModel(AddressManager(), (; Bus=bus, PQ=pq, PV=pv, Branch=branch))

    sol = solve_power_flow(sys)

    @test SciMLBase.successful_retcode(sol.retcode)
    @test norm(sol.resid, Inf) < 1e-6
end

Estimated effort: 4-6 hours

1.2 Per-Model Sparsity Refinement (Optional Optimization)

Goal: Allow models to declare finer-grained variable dependencies.

Current limitation: jacobian_sparsity_pattern assumes each residual depends on ALL variables of that instance. This is conservative - some variables might not affect certain residuals.

Implementation:

Add to src/powercore/model_var.jl:

"""
    residual_dependencies(::Type{Model}, residual_name::Symbol) -> Vector{Symbol}

Declare which variables a specific residual depends on.

Default: All variables (conservative but correct)
Models can override for tighter sparsity.

# Example
\```julia
# PQ residuals only depend on voltage magnitude, not angle
function residual_dependencies(::Type{PQ}, residual_name::Symbol)
    if residual_name == :p || residual_name == :q
        return [:v]  # Only voltage magnitude
    end
    return all_variables(PQ)  # Fallback
end
\```
"""
function residual_dependencies(::Type{M}, residual_name::Symbol) where M<:AbstractModel
    # Default: all variables
    meta = model_metadata(M)
    return [var.name for var in meta.vars]
end

Update src/powercore/sparsity_pattern.jl:

function jacobian_sparsity_pattern(sys::SystemModel; refined::Bool=false)
    # ... existing code ...

    for residual in metadata.residuals
        res_addrs = # ... get addresses ...

        if refined
            # Use model-specific dependencies
            dep_vars = residual_dependencies(base_type, residual.name)
            var_addr_lists_filtered = [var_addr_lists[i] for (i, var) in enumerate(metadata.vars)
                                       if var.name in dep_vars]
        else
            # Conservative: all variables
            var_addr_lists_filtered = var_addr_lists
        end

        # ... rest of loop ...
    end
end

Models to refine (examples):

  • PQ: Both p and q residuals only depend on voltage magnitude v (not angle theta)
  • Branch: Could separate which residuals depend on which bus angles
  • PV: v_ctrl residual only depends on local voltage

Estimated effort: 2-3 hours Expected benefit: 5-10% fewer nonzeros (marginal) Recommendation: Low priority - current conservative pattern works well

Priority 2: Alternative Autodiff Backends (Research, High Risk)

2.1 Reverse-Mode AD (Enzyme.jl or Zygote.jl)

Goal: For optimization problems where you need gradients of scalar objectives.

Use case: Optimal power flow, parameter estimation, objective = scalar cost function

Current state: ForwardDiff is great for Jacobians (many outputs from many inputs). For gradients (one output from many inputs), reverse-mode is more efficient.

Implementation sketch:

using Enzyme

"""
    compute_gradient(objective!, sys::SystemModel, y::Vector{Float64})

Compute ∇_y f(y) where f is a scalar objective function.

# Example
\```julia
# Minimize total generation cost
function objective!(cost, y, sys)
    # Evaluate residuals to get power flows
    cache = CachedAutodiffWorkspace(sys)
    g = similar(y)
    cache(g, y)

    # Extract generator outputs and compute cost
    cost[1] = sum(compute_cost(pgen))
end

grad = compute_gradient(objective!, sys, y)
\```
"""
function compute_gradient(objective!, sys::SystemModel, y::Vector{Float64})
    cost = [0.0]

    # Enzyme reverse-mode
    autodiff(Reverse, objective!, Duplicated(cost, [1.0]), Const(y), Const(sys))

    return # gradient (extracted from Enzyme)
end

Files to create:

  • src/powercore/reverse_autodiff.jl

Challenges:

  • Enzyme requires mutation-free code (our code mutates workspaces)
  • Would need to refactor for functional style
  • Zygote doesn't support mutation at all
  • Complex type interactions

Estimated effort: 2-3 weeks (research project) Recommendation: Only if you need optimization, not just power flow

2.2 GPU Autodiff (Enzyme.jl + CUDA)

Goal: Compute Jacobian on GPU using autodiff.

Current state:

  • We have GPU kernels for residuals (manual, fast)
  • No GPU autodiff yet

Why this is hard:

  • Enzyme.jl CUDA support is experimental
  • ForwardDiff doesn't support GPU arrays well
  • Would need to make entire workspace generic over Array types
  • Memory management is tricky with Dual numbers on GPU

Implementation notes:

Would require:

  1. Generic workspace over CuArray{Dual}
  2. Enzyme integration for CUDA kernels
  3. Careful memory management

Benchmark comparison needed:

  • Manual GPU Jacobian kernel (if implemented): ~fast
  • Enzyme GPU autodiff: ~unknown
  • CPU autodiff + data transfer: Current approach (~140ms for 135k system)

Estimated effort: 1-2 months (PhD-level research) Recommendation: Skip unless:

  • You implement manual analytical Jacobian and it's too slow on GPU
  • Enzyme CUDA support matures significantly
  • You have >1M variables

Priority 3: Symbolic/Analytical Jacobian (Alternative Approach)

3.1 Symbolics.jl Integration

Goal: Use Symbolics.jl to compute sparsity pattern (alternative to our structural approach).

Current state: We use model structure. Symbolics would trace execution symbolically.

Implementation:

using Symbolics

function jacobian_sparsity_symbolic(sys::SystemModel)
    cache = CachedAutodiffWorkspace(sys)
    y = copy(cache.sys.dae.y)
    g = similar(y)

    # Symbolics traces execution
    sparsity = Symbolics.jacobian_sparsity(
        (g, y) -> cache(g, y),
        g, y
    )

    return sparsity
end

Pros:

  • Automatic (no manual pattern declaration)
  • Handles complex control flow

Cons:

  • Slower than structural approach (~100ms vs <1ms)
  • Requires tracing through entire evaluation
  • More dependencies

Recommendation: Our structural approach is faster and simpler. Only use Symbolics if:

  • Model structure is too complex to analyze
  • You want cross-validation of sparsity patterns

Estimated effort: 2-3 hours Expected benefit: Validation tool, not production

3.2 Analytical Jacobian Generation

Goal: Derive analytical Jacobian formulas and implement directly (no autodiff).

Example for PQ model:

function analytical_jacobian_pq!(J::AbstractMatrix, pq::PQVec, y::Vector{Float64}, ...)
    # Hand-derived formulas
    # ∂p/∂v = -(ip + 2*yp*v)
    # ∂q/∂v = -(iq + 2*yq*v)

    for i in 1:length(pq)
        v_idx = get_voltage_index(i)
        p_idx = get_p_residual_index(i)
        q_idx = get_q_residual_index(i)

        J[p_idx, v_idx] = -(pq.ip[i] + 2 * pq.yp[i] * y[v_idx])
        J[q_idx, v_idx] = -(pq.iq[i] + 2 * pq.yq[i] * y[v_idx])
    end
end

Pros:

  • Fastest possible (no autodiff overhead)
  • Educational (see exact formulas)
  • Ultimate performance

Cons:

  • Manual work for every model
  • Error-prone (easy to make mistakes in derivatives)
  • Maintenance burden (code changes require derivative updates)

Recommendation: Implement if:

  • Autodiff is proven bottleneck (unlikely after our optimizations)
  • You want ultimate performance
  • You have test cases to validate against autodiff

Files to create:

  • src/models/pq_jacobian.jl
  • src/models/pv_jacobian.jl
  • src/models/branch_jacobian.jl
  • src/powercore/analytical_jacobian.jl (dispatcher)

Estimated effort: 1-2 weeks Expected speedup: 2-3x over autodiff (diminishing returns)

How to Pick Up This Work

For NonlinearSolve.jl Integration

  1. Read these files first:

    • src/analysis/autodiff_cache.jl - Understand CachedAutodiffWorkspace
    • src/powercore/sparsity_pattern.jl - Understand sparsity detection
    • examples/autodiff_success.jl - See usage patterns

  2. Install dependencies:

    using Pkg
Pkg.add("NonlinearSolve")

  3. Create the solver file:

    touch src/solvers/nonlinear_solve.jl

  4. Start with the basic wrapper:

    • Wrap CachedAutodiffWorkspace as a NonlinearFunction
    • Pass sparsity pattern to jac_prototype
    • Test on IEEE 14-bus first

  5. Reference implementation:

    • See NonlinearSolve.jl docs: https://docs.sciml.ai/NonlinearSolve/stable/
    • Look at sparse Jacobian examples in their tutorials

For Per-Model Sparsity Refinement

  1. Understand current implementation:

    • Read jacobian_sparsity_pattern in src/powercore/sparsity_pattern.jl
    • Note how it loops over models and variables

  2. Add the trait:

    • Define residual_dependencies in src/powercore/model_var.jl
    • Default implementation returns all variables

  3. Refine PQ model (easiest):

    # In src/models/pq.jl
function Powerful.residual_dependencies(::Type{PQ}, residual_name::Symbol)
    return [:v]  # Both p and q only depend on voltage magnitude
end

  4. Test:

    • Compare sparsity before/after
    • Validate Jacobian values match

For Analytical Jacobian

  1. Benchmark first:

    • Profile current autodiff Jacobian
    • Identify if it's actually a bottleneck
    • Get baseline times

  2. Start with PQ (simplest model):

    • Derive ∂p/∂v and ∂q/∂v by hand
    • Implement in src/models/pq_jacobian.jl
    • Test against autodiff output

  3. Validation is critical:

    using Test

J_auto = compute_jacobian_autodiff(sys, y)
J_anal = compute_jacobian_analytical(sys, y)

@test maximum(abs.(J_auto - J_anal)) < 1e-10

Testing Strategy

For any new feature, add tests:

# test/test_new_feature.jl
@testitem "Feature Name" begin
    using Powerful, PowerFlowData

    # Load test case
    case = PowerFlowData.parse_network(...)
    sys = create_system(case)

    # Test feature
    result = new_feature(sys)

    # Validate
    @test is_correct(result)
end

Run tests:

julia --project -e 'using TestItemRunner; @run_package_tests'

Performance Benchmarking

Always benchmark against current implementation:

using BenchmarkTools

# Current approach
cache = CachedAutodiffWorkspace(sys)
sparsity = jacobian_sparsity_pattern(sys)
colors = matrix_colors(sparsity)
J = Float64.(sparsity)

@benchmark forwarddiff_color_jacobian!($J, $cache, $y0; colorvec=$colors)

# New approach
@benchmark new_jacobian_method!($J, $sys, $y0)

# Compare

Documentation Requirements

For any implemented feature:

  1. Docstrings - All public functions
  2. Examples - At least one working example
  3. Tests - Unit tests + integration test
  4. Performance - Benchmark vs baseline
  5. README update - Add to main README if user-facing

Questions?

If picking up this work:

  1. Check examples/autodiff_success.jl for usage patterns
  2. Run examples/large_system_jacobian.jl for performance baseline
  3. File issues at: https://github.com/user/Powerful.jl/issues

Summary

What's done: Full autodiff integration with sparse Jacobians (~140ms for 135k variables)

What's recommended next: NonlinearSolve.jl integration (4-6 hours, high value)

What's optional: Everything else is optimization or research

Current performance is production-ready - remaining work is about API convenience and edge case optimization, not core functionality.
